scoreNote: Strong (5): argues the policy should be adopted because the economic gain forgone is temporary while the wilderness lost is permanent, and a firm law resists piecemeal erosion, while qualifying the absolute 'any' with narrow exceptions for genuine need.

sentences.text: When a forest can be felled for timber or a marsh drained for farmland, the wealth is tempting and the loss is easy to ignore — until it is too late.
The proposed policy meets that temptation head-on, urging nations to pass laws preserving any remaining wilderness in its natural state, even where the land could be developed for economic gain.

The policy is, on balance, wise and should be adopted, because the economic gain it forgoes is temporary while the wilderness it protects is irreplaceable; its one real weakness is the word any, which ought to admit narrow exceptions for genuine human necessity.
The heart of the policy is sound because the choice it addresses is between the temporary and the permanent.
Economic gain from developing wilderness is real but finite — the timber is sold, the mine is exhausted, the profit is spent — whereas the wilderness destroyed to obtain it is gone for good.
Because the loss is irreversible and the gain is fleeting, a law that errs on the side of preservation protects future generations who will have no chance to undo today's clearing.
Adopting the policy trades a passing profit for a permanent inheritance, which is usually a wise bargain.

sections.role: Body — A firm law resists erosion

sentences.text: Furthermore, the likely consequences of leaving wilderness unprotected make the case stronger still.
Without a firm law, each wild area is decided case by case, and short-term economic pressure almost always wins, so wilderness is lost in incremental pieces until little remains.
Wilderness also provides services no development can replace — clean water, a stable climate, biodiversity, and refuge — whose value markets routinely fail to count.
A standing law that says no by default corrects this bias, forcing a nation to weigh the true, long-term worth of wild land against the immediate profit of destroying it.
The policy's great advantage is that it resists the steady, piecemeal erosion that unprotected wilderness always suffers.
However, the policy's blanket word any goes a step too far.
A poor nation may sometimes face genuine necessity — land truly needed to feed, house, or power its people — and an absolute, exceptionless ban would ignore those legitimate human claims.
A wiser law would preserve wilderness as the strong default while allowing rare, carefully justified exceptions, rather than forbidding every use of every acre regardless of circumstance.
This preserves the policy's real strength — a heavy presumption against development — while avoiding the rigidity that would discredit it and invite evasion.
Adopt the policy's firm protection, but build in narrow, honest exceptions for true necessity.
In conclusion, nations should adopt this policy, for preserving wilderness even at an economic cost is usually the wiser long-term choice.

The gain from developing wild land is temporary and the loss permanent, and only a firm law can resist the constant pressure to trade the irreplaceable for a quick profit, so the policy is advantageous wherever it sets a strong presumption for preservation while allowing narrow exceptions for genuine need.
Forgo the easy profit and keep the wilderness; the gain would be spent in a generation, but the loss would last forever.
